strengths: Strong empirical results with state-of-the-art performance on both ScreenSpot-v2 (93.9%) and ScreenSpot-Pro (56.5%), particularly the +6.4% improvement on the more challenging benchmark
Well-motivated problem formulation: identifies genuine limitation of one-step GUI grounding methods (absence of visual feedback) and proposes intuitive interactive solution
Thorough experimental analysis including effective ablation studies, detailed training dynamics analysis with identified three-stage learning, and insightful cursor-in-box spatial reasoning test
Practical engineering contributions: cursor-centric focusing (CCF) strategy effective for high-resolution images, well-designed trajectory penalties preventing degenerate behaviors
Comprehensive baseline comparisons across both supervised fine-tuning and RL-based methods with detailed performance breakdown by UI categories
Adaptive movement strategy: model learns to use single steps for most examples but intelligently conducts more steps for difficult (small target) cases
Good presentation with clear writing, informative visualizations, and accessible methodology explanation with detailed implementation details
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily task reformulation + straightforward reward function design using standard GRPO, rather than methodological innovation; trajectory penalties are somewhat obvious solutions to prevent degenerate behaviors

Narrow evaluation scope: only two related benchmarks (ScreenSpot variants); no evaluation on other major GUI grounding datasets (Mind2Web, WebShop, MiniWoB++); no cross-domain or out-of-distribution tests

Generalization concerns: zero-shot performance collapses dramatically (88.8% → 36.3% with direct move), suggesting benefits are almost entirely from RL fine-tuning rather than learned robust spatial understanding; only tested with single base model

Contradiction between claims and evidence: paper claims multi-step movement is key contribution, but 95% of examples use single-step on ScreenSpot-v2 and only 9.4% use >1 step on ScreenSpot-Pro; benefits appear to come primarily from single-step improvement with visual feedback

CCF strategy has fundamental limitation: ~10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples have targets outside the focused area when initial prediction is poor; improvements on other baselines smaller (GTA1/GUI-G2: +3.9% each) when CCF applied separately

Hyperparameter choices lack justification: trajectory penalty weight wp=0.2 with higher false stop penalty 0.5 appears ad-hoc; no sensitivity analysis; cursor size (20×31) arbitrary with no ablations; format reward weight 0.1 unjustified

Training efficiency not thoroughly evaluated: requires 8 A100 GPUs but total training time not specified; computational cost comparison with baselines absent; impact of sampling multiple trajectories per example not quantified

Incomplete analysis of spatial reasoning: cursor-in-box improvement modest and causality unclear; claim that visual feedback improves general spatial understanding undermined by model's poor zero-shot performance; improvements may reflect task-specific overfitting rather than robust reasoning
Limited failure analysis: few negative examples in appendix; concerning behaviors (hallucinating action sequences, repeated predictions) not systematically analyzed or categorized

Training-inference mismatch and reproducibility concerns: resolution mismatch (1920×1080 training vs 4096×2160 testing); max steps mismatch (4 training vs flexible inference); online filtering and preprocessing may prevent exact reproduction; code release not mentioned

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving SOTA on ScreenSpot-v2 (93.9%) and ScreenSpot-Pro (56.5%) with 6.4% improvement over prior SOTA
Well-motivated problem formulation identifying the lack of visual feedback in one-step coordinate prediction approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including thorough ablations, cursor-in-box spatial reasoning analysis, and detailed case studies
Insightful findings that even strong base models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) exhibit positional bias in spatial reasoning and that training improves this without explicit training
Practical cursor-centric focusing (CCF) strategy that effectively handles high-resolution images during inference
Generally clear presentation with good organization and extensive implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: approach straightforwardly combines existing techniques (GRPO, position reward from SE-GUI, standard trajectory penalties) without novel algorithmic contributions

Critical confounding issue: the 11.2 percentage point improvement from CCF (45.3% → 56.5%) dominates the total gains, making it unclear whether interactive reasoning or engineering (CCF strategy) is the key driver
Missing crucial ablation: no direct comparison of interactive training vs. one-step training on identical setup (same base model, resolution, data) to isolate the interactive component's contribution

Confounded experimental setup: GUI-CURSOR trains at 1920×1080 while GTA1 trains at 4096×2160, making direct comparison problematic
Known failure mode dismissed: 10.3% of ScreenSpot-Pro examples have targets outside the focused area with no solution proposed
Unclear mechanistic understanding of improvements: thinking tokens shown to help but no analysis of what spatial reasoning they actually perform
Spatial reasoning improvements modest and possibly epiphenomenal: cursor-in-box test is artificial and improvement not explicitly trained for; unclear if it transfers to better grounding

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Reframing GUI grounding as interactive cursor movement with visual feedback is creative and well-motivated, addressing real limitations of one-step prediction methods
Strong empirical results: Achieves SOTA on both benchmarks with particularly impressive 29.7% improvement on ScreenSpot-Pro (26.8% → 56.5%), beating prior SOTA GTA1 by 5.8%
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough ablation studies, movement step analysis showing adaptive behavior, zero-shot experiments, and detailed case studies provide strong validation
Insightful analysis: The cursor-in-box test effectively demonstrates that base models lack robust spatial understanding, and that GUI-CURSOR improves this capability without explicit training
Practical technical contributions: Cursor-centric focusing (CCF) strategy elegantly balances training efficiency with inference accuracy; trajectory penalty design prevents degenerate behaviors
Clear presentation and reproducibility: Well-written with informative figures, logical flow, detailed implementation details in appendices, and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Modest improvements on primary benchmark: Only 1.5% gain over GTA1 on ScreenSpot-v2 (93.9% vs 92.4%), raising questions about generalization across difficulty levels

Unclear attribution of improvements: Zero-shot results show Qwen-2.5-VL-7B performs worse with cursor movement (36.3% vs 88.8%), suggesting benefits may come primarily from improved RL rewards rather than inherent spatial reasoning from interactive environment

Ad-hoc design choices lacking justification: Trajectory penalty weights (0.2, with 0.5 for false stop), maximum 4 movement steps, and specific penalty formulations appear empirically chosen without principled rationale or sensitivity analysis

CCF strategy limitations: Known failure mode affecting 10.3% of examples; appears to be a workaround for computational constraints rather than principled solution; also trains at lower resolution than some baselines
Limited technical novelty: GRPO is standard; trajectory penalties are somewhat ad-hoc; main contribution is problem reformulation rather than algorithmic innovation
High computational requirements: Needs 8 A100 80GB GPUs for training, limiting reproducibility and accessibility
Missing comparative analysis: No controlled comparison with simpler baseline using GRPO on single-step predictions to isolate benefits of interactive environment vs. better rewards

Comprehensive implementation details and reproducibility information provided in extensive appendices

Thorough ablation studies and detailed supplementary analysis including training dynamics and spatial reasoning diagnosis

Clean presentation of the interactive environment formulation with illustrative examples

Critical contribution conflation: Cannot isolate whether gains come from multi-step training, visual feedback mechanism, specific reward penalties, or CCF strategy

Exceptionally comprehensive evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, ScreenSpot-v2) with diverse baselines and online agentic evaluation; strong empirical results (8.1% improvement over GTA1 with 8× fewer training samples)
Thoughtfully designed trajectory-aware reward function with four well-justified penalties; systematic ablations validate each component's contribution

Insightful analysis including cursor-in-box test demonstrating base model spatial reasoning deficits, analysis showing adaptive multi-step behavior on harder examples, and evidence of improved OOD spatial reasoning generalization
Practical cursor-centric focusing (CCF) strategy elegantly balances training efficiency with inference accuracy on varied resolution inputs
Excellent presentation with clear writing, informative visualizations, and detailed case studies; thorough appendices support reproducibility
Data efficiency advantage: achieves state-of-the-art results with only 8K training samples versus 64K for GTA1, demonstrating sample efficiency benefits
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (GRPO from prior work, standard reward engineering); main contribution is problem reformulation and empirical validation rather than methodological innovation

Non-trivial computational efficiency trade-offs inadequately emphasized: 2.4× longer training time (680s vs 289s per step), +0.3s inference latency increase, 12.5% throughput reduction—costs that complicate practical deployment
